Oil Rebounds Toward $100 as Democrats' Sweep Rattles Energy Stocks
sum: Oil prices reversed their recent downtrend on Thursday, a day after Democrats swept control of both the House and Senate, creating a potential legislative check on U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration. Brent crude was up 4.0% to trade at $98.38 per barrel at 3:15 pm ET, while WTI gained 2.9% to $90.65, with prices rising for the first time in four sessions after plunging to a near two-month low on Wednesday. U.S. natural gas prices were flat at $2.95/MMBtu, while European gas prices rebounded 1.9% to €89.72/MWh. The U.S. stock market resumed its recent downtrend on Thursday, with the S&P 500 down more than 3% and the Nasdaq off about 5% in afternoon trading as a selloff in AI chip stocks deepened. AI stocks tied to Texas data centers were hit hard after Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated long-serving Texas governor Greg Abbott, with CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) falling 7% and Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) each sliding 4% in overnight trading on Wednesday. Hinojosa has called for a pause on new data-center projects until protections for electricity supplies, water resources and local communities are in place, with investors fearing similar roadblocks could slow down the AI data center boom once Democratic governors take office in January 2027.

The energy investment universe was a mixed bag, with the oil and gas benchmark, State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE), falling 1.6% to $62.50 on Thursday, as energy stocks tracked the broader market lower despite the rebound in crude. Wednesday’s 8.7% plunge in Brent priced in bets that the election setback would force the Trump administration to pursue a peace deal with Iran and reopen Hormuz.

Those bets faded on Thursday, with Eurasia Group cutting its odds of a negotiated agreement to 10% from 20% and putting the likelihood of renewed U.S. strikes at 60%, while Iran’s navy reported that a tanker struck a mine east of the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire. President Trump acknowledged the war’s role in the Republican losses but said the conflict has been worth it.
Additionally, Democratic committee chairs are set to deploy their new subpoena powers from January to investigate the administration’s energy dealings.

Saudi Aramco Q3 profit jumps 34.5% to $36.25 billion despite ongoing US-Iran conflict
sum: The world's largest oil exporter posted net profit of $36.25 billion for the three months ended September 30, compared with $26.9 billion in the same period last year. This was also higher than the $32.7 billion recorded in the second quarter.

Adjusted net income stood at approximately $31.2 billion, beating the median analyst estimate of $30.66 billion, based on a consensus shared by Aramco from 12 analysts.

Higher oil prices helped offset the impact of reduced production volumes caused by the US-Iran war. The conflict has disrupted Aramco's output while increasing security risks for Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure.

Other Saudi energy infrastructure and Aramco's headquarters have also come under attack as fighting intensified in the wider regional conflict involving Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group.
The latest results highlight how higher crude prices have helped Aramco cushion the financial impact of production disruptions and mounting security risks.

items.t: 3 Private Deals Executed on the Saudi Stock Exchange, Valued at SAR 49 Million
sum: On Monday, November 2, 2026, three private deals were executed on the Saudi Stock Exchange ("Tadawul"), involving 2.2 million shares of Saudi Aramco, Saudi Electrical Industries, and AlAhli Bank. The total value of these transactions reached approximately SAR 49 million.

A private transaction occurs when both the seller and the buyer agree upon the quantity and price of the listed securities involved. Regarding settlement, these negotiated transactions can be settled within a timeframe ranging from T+0 to T+5, as agreed upon by the parties; if no specific settlement period is determined by the seller and buyer, a T+2 settlement cycle is applied automatically.

Furthermore, transactions executed during any additional trading sessions must comply with daily price fluctuation limits and minimum transaction value requirements. Negotiated transactions may be carried out during the following sessions: the pre-opening auction, the open market session, the closing auction, the market-closed session, and the post-closing session.

The pre-opening auction and post-closing sessions are made available once the lead underwriter or the transaction coordinator submits a formal request and fulfills all requirements set by the Saudi Stock Exchange (Tadawul) for enabling these sessions.

Google, Nvidia Led $3.17T AI Stock Slide; Only Four Rose
sum: Thirty large AI-exposed stocks lost a combined $3.17 trillion of market value in October, from $37.53 trillion at the end of September to $34.36 trillion at the close on 30 October, an 8.5% fall by our arithmetic. Only four of the 30 rose.

Alphabet, Google’s parent, and Nvidia together lost $1.35 trillion, 43% of the total. The gainers were Tesla, Apple, Microsoft and IBM, and the month ended on the day Apple passed Nvidia as the most valuable company.
A short Business Engineer explainer on power laws, where a few outcomes account for most of the value. It teaches the general idea only and does not discuss the companies in this story.

By our arithmetic, Alphabet lost $780.2 billion (18.5%), Nvidia $572.1 billion (10.4%), Intel $289.5 billion (45.3%), Meta $281.7 billion (15.2%) and Micron $204.1 billion (16.9%). Those five account for $2.13 trillion, or 67% of the group’s fall.

Memory makers fell together: Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics lost a combined $549.5 billion. Chip-equipment makers Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA and ASML lost $350.9 billion between them.

The steepest percentage falls were Intel at 45.3%, CoreWeave at 37.0%, Arm at 28.9% and Lam Research at 27.2%. Intel’s shares fell 28.6% on 30 October alone after its results, as we reported on Friday.
Tesla added $177.9 billion (12.7%), Apple $169.4 billion (3.5%), Microsoft $66.9 billion (1.8%) and IBM $35.8 billion (17.2%), by our arithmetic. Salesforce was close to flat, down $0.3 billion.
